                   COMMENTS OF THE TEXAS ENERGY BUYERS ALLIANCE

                                           I.    INTRODUCTION

        The Texas Energy Buyers Alliance (TEBA) represents the collective voice of more than 200

companies, representing some of the state’s largest employers and energy customers. In total, TEBA

members represent more than $36 trillion in market capitalization and hundreds of thousands of employees

in Texas. Our organization is focused on helping to shape Texas’ electricity market redesign in ways that

propel Texas’ economy forward, lower power bills for all energy customers, create jobs, spur innovation,

strengthen the ERCOT grid, and extend Texas’ energy leadership through the energy transition and for

generations to come.

        Because TEBA’s membership represents such a unique cross-section of the businesses in Texas,

we feel we are uniquely qualified to provide insight into this question. Hyperscaler data centers, retail

businesses, petrochemical companies, technology companies, and manufacturers make up our membership

and share a common purpose to protect the efficient, reliable, low-cost ERCOT market. As direct purchasers

and operators of some of the largest and most complex loads in ERCOT, TEBA members have firsthand

experience with the challenges of integrating new large loads and are well positioned to provide practical

guidance on the implementation of Senate Bill 6 (SB6). Our broad membership, which extends beyond

these new large loads, continues to need efficient markets that deliver reliable operations, low costs, and

ongoing economic opportunities.

        New large loads will result in a new major round of investments in transmission and generation

infrastructure that will lower costs for all consumers if there are no barriers put in place for investments in

low-cost resources. TEBA emphasizes that the integration of new large loads must be approached with a

balanced framework that both safeguards reliability and encourages economic investment across the state

 of Texas. Transparent and predictable interconnection processes are critical to ensuring that Texas remains

competitive in attracting large load customers.

        TEBA recognizes the nuances in implementing SB6’s requirements and appreciates the time and

effort that Commission staff has dedicated to solving this important puzzle.

          II.    RESPONSES TO COMMISSION STAFF’S QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

        TEBA appreciates the opportunity to provide comments in response to the Commission staff’s

second set of questions and discussion draft language for Project No. 58481. We respectfully submit the

following responses for consideration by the Public Utility Commission of Texas.



        Question 1: Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load

        customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how should the

        commission define those parameters?

        Yes, the Commission should define more specific parameters for substantially similar

interconnection requests, as doing so will provide clarity and consistency in evaluating large load projects.

While many projects may appear similar on the surface, our members expect ongoing demand for large

loads will make “duplicative” projects substitutable for other needs. Clearly asked questions will help avoid

confusion for large loads and provide valuable information for planners, while vague standards will risk

discouraging developers from investing in new projects in Texas.

        A practical way to meet this objective is to ask whether the approval of one project would directly

cause another to be canceled, reduced in scale, or delayed. This question provides a straightforward measure

of whether two requests are functionally overlapping or mutually exclusive. By focusing on the impact of

energization approval, the Commission can get clear answers to the intent of the duplicative load question

asked by the authors of SB6.

        It is important, however, that if a large load customer discloses that they are pursuing a

substantially similar load, they are not placed at a disadvantage. The rulemaking should ensure that the

response to this disclosure does not delay, impair, or otherwise disadvantage projects that may be

considering or pursuing substantially similar interconnection requests, so long as they meet all

requirements to proceed with the large load interconnection study.

         Question 2: Proposed subsection (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific

        information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows a large

        load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the commission list what

        is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not competitively sensitive

        information)? If so, what information should and should not be considered competitively

        sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is a

        duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to materialize?

        Information tied to commercial transactions should remain confidential, as disclosure of such

details could compromise competitive positions and discourage investment. The customer is in the best

position to determine this. It is unclear in the draft whether this information would be aggregated and

published or not, and so answering that first-order question would facilitate what information should be

considered competitively sensitive or not.



        Question 3: Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the

        interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially

        disclosed in response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed? If

        only material changes, how should “material change” be defined?

        Notification should be required only for material changes that have the potential to impact the

results of the large load interconnection study. This ensures that ERCOT and the interconnecting utility

are informed of developments that could alter transmission planning or system reliability, while avoiding

unnecessary administrative burdens for customers.

        Material changes should be defined as those that result in significant impacts on the project. TEBA

emphasizes that flexibility is critical, as many large load customers are unable to specify exact operational

characteristics at the early stages of the process. ERCOT should accept generic disclosures to allow

projects to advance, with the understanding that more precise information will be provided as the project



                                                      5
 matures. A large load could serve a variety of purposes over time, and the transmission system needs to

be robust enough to manage this.

          Ultimately, the Commission should permit some flexibility to ensure that projects are not overly

burdened and delayed by minor project adjustments. Establishing a practical threshold for what constitutes

a material change will help balance the need for transparency with the realities of project development,

allowing the interconnection process to move forward efficiently.



          Question 4: Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting electric utility to

          refund 20% of a large load customer’s security after energization and ratably as the large

          load customer meets the milestone identified in the customer’s schedule for phased

          energization (e.g. 20% for each year of operations until the full amount of security is

          refunded)? If so, how should the commission standardize the refund?

          TEBA proposes a major alternative to the treatment of financial security offered by Commission

staff. TEBA believes that holding customer funds for extended periods provides limited public value and

will hinder economic growth. It is important that the Commission prioritize a refund system that returns

funds to customers as quickly as possible to comply with SB6, which strongly emphasizes economic

growth.

          To prioritize returning capital to the interconnecting customer, the proposed payment and refund

timeline should be completely restructured. First, the $/MW security should be paid at the same time as

the study fee, and then either refunded once the CIAC is paid or applied directly toward the CIAC. This

approach allows the security to be used as a “show of strength” before the utility begins its interconnection

study and reduces the burden on utilities that are overwhelmed with project requests today. Many utilities

are falling behind schedule on interconnection studies, and this approach could reduce the number of

studies they are responsible for and ultimately reduce their workload.

          Besides the show of strength, the primary purpose of the $/MW security as proposed in this

discussion draft is to ensure that new loads pay their transmission costs. TEBA agrees with concerns about

                                                      6
 “phantom load,” or the risk of planning and building transmission upgrades for projects that ultimately do

not materialize. However, any costs incurred by the utility could be taken from the financial security before

issuing a refund if a project is canceled. If a project moves forward to energization, then costs would be

recovered through the CIAC and TCOS payments instead of the financial security. In this scenario, the

risk of non-payment is accounted for at each step of the process without holding the $/MW financial

security for years after energization by relying on CIAC and TCOS payments instead.

          Considering this, it is TEBA’s understanding that the discussion draft assumes that holding the

$/MW value past the energization date would ensure that the large load is paying for transmission costs

after interconnection. TEBA has proposed a solution in the TCOS project that would allow the $/MW

security to be refunded earlier while also ensuring that transmission costs are covered. Our proposal would

establish a minimum demand charge for several years, ensuring that new large loads pay a significant

portion of transmission costs. If adopted, this proposal would simplify both the TCOS reform and

streamline this rule, as unavoidable TCOS payments would substitute for holding the $/MW security for

years after energization. In this scenario, transmission costs are guaranteed to be paid (regardless of CP

methodology), and the security could be refunded much earlier.

          Furthermore, there would be no need to determine whether specific transmission lines primarily

benefit one particular customer and should be directly assigned. The discussion draft’s suggestion to

pursue such determinations via CIAC is a cause of concern. Texas has been long recognized for

maintaining simple wholesale transmission cost allocation through postage stamp pricing, which avoids

drawn-out disagreements regarding who should pay for a transmission line and the associated project

delays. Importantly, postage stamp wholesale transmission rates are required by PURA.1

          In conjunction with the transmission cost proposal in the TCOS docket, TEBA believes the

financial structure should be as follows:

If the Commission follows this recommendation, each of the financial requirements in this rulemaking and

        Question 5: Are changes to the commission’s other substantive rules necessary to align with

        this rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?

        Yes. Broadly, all SB6 rulemakings are very interconnected. As emphasized above, TEBA believes

that this rulemaking is tied closely to the TCOS rulemaking. It is also related to the “Criteria in the ERCOT

Load Forecast” rulemaking, as the requirements for inclusion in the load forecast seem to closely align

with the requirements set forth in the discretionary services agreement. These should be cross-checked to

ensure they align with 100% accuracy. We recommend that the Commission set an overall approach

to these policy questions soon, and then let the rulemakings derive from that policy approach.

         TEBA proposes several edits to the definitions in subsection (b). The definitions for “project

developer” and “end-use customer” should be cut. As used in the discussion draft, the definition is far too

limiting and will not provide value in the interconnection process. Developers often work on behalf of

end-use customers and, in some cases, are long-term partners. Moreover, identifying whether a large load

customer is an end-use customer does not meaningfully inform that interconnection process. While

Commission staff may see large loads with a defined end-use customer as being more “viable,” a

customer may still decide to delay or downsize a project based on their own needs, like cash flow, and

whether the product they will make at the site has offtake agreements or is subject to larger market trends.

Furthermore, there isn’t a clearly established use for this information in the discussion draft. If the

intention is to validate load requests, the definitions and language as currently written would not

accomplish this goal unless the Commission requests far more information. For these reasons, TEBA

proposes eliminating all references to “project developer” and “end-use customer,” as they are irrelevant

and outside the scope of SB6 requirements.

        In the definition of large load interconnection studies, TEBA suggests adding the sentence, “The

large load interconnection process should be a standardized process across all interconnecting utilities.”

Broadly, a standardized process across utilities would reduce confusion, shorten timelines, and ensure

consistent treatment of large load customers across the state. It would additionally improve transparency

and predictability for developers while easing administrative burdens on ERCOT. Regarding the proposed

language, we recognize that “should be” is rarely used in Commission rules. We propose it deliberately.

A requirement that the procedures “must” be standardized would make change very difficult and could

cause further delay while utilities work together to create a standardized process. “Should be” provides

guidance and expresses desire without creating a new regulatory barrier.

        Additionally, “pre-screening study” must be defined as we suggest inserting the concept into the

process. It’s important that large load customers who are considering multi-million-dollar financial

security decisions have access to a quick, high-level assessment of site viability before they post their

security and pay for the full interconnection study. The primary purpose of a pre-screen study is to

requirements of their project at a specific location on the grid, helping them make informed decisions

while minimizing burdens on utilities. We believe the addition of this concept is necessary because our

proposal moves the financial security posting requirements before the utility’s interconnection study, as

explained further in the coming sections.

        Finally, we note that the discussion draft skipped (b)(8). We identify this omission to assist in

future drafting.

        TEBA proposes significant restructuring of subsection (c) to accomplish our primary objective:

requiring the $/MW financial security before the utility’s interconnection study begins. This change allows

for the complete deletion of subsection (e), with necessary language from (e) to be added herein. To reflect

this restructuring, TEBA recommends modifying the title of subsection (c) and revising the introductory

language appropriately.

        Consistent with our broader comments, TEBA suggests eliminating the identification requirement

for developers or end-use customers. Accordingly, subsection (c)(1) should be deleted, resulting in

renumbering throughout the entire section. For clarity, TEBA will reference both the original subsection

and the renumbered subsection.

        In subsection (c)(2)(renumbered 1), addressing site control, TEBA recommends adding a fourth

option: an exclusivity agreement with an existing generator for a co-location arrangement. If the end-use

customer is the sole user of the interconnection facilities, this should be considered an adequate



                                                      18
 demonstration of site control. It is also suggested that “legally binding” be deleted from the option

requirement, as all agreements are presumed to be legally binding.

        In subsection (c)(3)(renumbered 2), we propose conforming edits to align with SB6 and other

sections within this rule. This includes noting that the requirement for notification of “substantially similar”

load requests is specifically within the state, allowing anonymization of information, and prohibiting its

sale. We also recommend narrowing the question about “substantially similar” requests (consistent with

our response to Question 1) to elicit more useful information. In addition, staff should pose more targeted

questions about the nature of substantially similar interconnection requests and set thresholds to determine

whether the answers to the substantially similar questions would have a material impact. For example, they

could ask to what extent energization of one project might delay another request, or how significantly it

might reduce the size of another. If a project’s reduction or delay does not exceed an established materiality

threshold, this provision should not apply. Asking whether the approval of one project would directly cause

another to be canceled, reduced in scale, or delayed would elicit more useful information. Finally, we

propose language ensuring that a customer’s interconnection rights are protected regardless of the answer

to this question.

        In subsection (c)(4)(renumbered 3), TEBA recommends replacing the word “expected” with

“desired” when disclosing the ramp schedule. At this stage of the interconnection process, the ramp

schedule is entirely dependent on utility and ERCOT actions, but the customer can confidently express their

desired schedule.

        In subsection (c)(6)(renumbered 5), TEBA proposes adding a sentence to reflect the reality of the

interconnection process. We propose adding: “At this stage of the interconnection process, the dynamic

modeling should be treated as an approximation.” Dynamic models are expected to mimic precise details

for how a facility will react under duress, but early in the process, they are inherently uncertain. Particularly,



                                                       19
 this early in the process, it is unlikely that a model for a proposed large load will be completely accurate.

This clarification would help set appropriate expectations for utilities, ERCOT, and policymakers.

        In subsection (c)(7)(renumbered 6), TEBA notes that the draft does not specify who receives the

study fee. Language clarifying that the study fee is paid to the utility is therefore added. We also suggest

the executive director’s choice to use an alternative to the CPI should extend beyond mere unavailability.

The methodology for publishing economic data seems to be in a period of change, and so broader discretion

may be prudent. We also reorganize the language so that the sentence on “combined costs” stands alone, as

it is not related to the annual adjustment of the fee. We also clarify that this adjustment would have to be

determined by the utility rather than the executive director.

        TEBA urges the Commission to make use of our proposal to allow third-party studies. Third-party

studies and third-party reviews are widely recognized policies to enable more efficient permitting across

multiple sectors. It is commonly known to the Commission and the industry that the large load

interconnection requests have created a historically large burden on interconnecting utilities. Granting

customers the right to pay for third-party studies is an essential reform to improve efficiency.

        Finally, in proposed subsection (c)(7) (the new financial security provision, incorporating language

from deleted subsection (e)), TEBA highlights three key edits to the original language. First, the study fee

was lowered from $50,000 to $25,000. While we understand that the security is intentionally high to deter

speculative businesses, $50,000 per MW is so high that it will discourage legitimate development. Second,

          II.    RESPONSES TO COMMISSION STAFF'S QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

        TEBA appreciates the opportunity to provide comments in response to the Commission staff's

second set of questions and discussion draft language for Project No. 58481. We respectfully submit the

following responses for consideration by the Public Utility Commission of Texas.



        Question 1: Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load

        customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how should the

        commission define those parameters?

        Yes, the Commission should define more specific parameters for substantially similar

interconnection requests, as doing so will provide clarity and consistency in evaluating large load projects.

While many projects may appear similar on the surface, our members expect ongoing demand for large

loads will make "duplicative" projects substitutable for other needs. Clearly asked questions will help avoid

confusion for large loads and provide valuable information for planners, while vague standards will risk

discouraging developers from investing in new projects in Texas.

        A practical way to meet this objective is to ask whether the approval of one project would directly

cause anotherto be canceled, reduced in scale, or delayed. This question provides a straightforward measure

of whether two requests are functionally overlapping or mutually exclusive. By focusing on the impact of

energization approval, the Commission can get clear answers to the intent ofthe duplicative load question

asked by the authors of SB6.

        It is important, however, that if a large load customer discloses that they are pursuing a

substantially similar load, they are not placed at a disadvantage. The rulemaking should ensure that the

response to this disclosure does not delay, impair, or otherwise disadvantage projects that may be

considering or pursuing substantially similar interconnection requests, so long as they meet all

requirements to proceed with the large load interconnection study.
